summary: High accuracy is not the same as fair outcomes, and confusing the two is one of the costliest mistakes in AI. Picture this. A company pilots an AI system that screens job applicants and recommends who should advance to the next round. The team runs tests and sees an overall prediction accuracy of 89%. Everyone is pleased. Then someone slices the results by demographic group. The rate at which the system recommends applicants differs by more than 20% across groups. The model is “accurate,” so what went wrong? Accuracy answers a different question Accuracy measures how often a model’s predictions match the labels it was trained on. It doesn’t ask whether those labels were fair to begin with. Suppose the training data is a decade of historical hiring decisions. If those decisions systematically favored some groups, a model that learns them well will score high on accuracy precisely because it has learned to imitate the bias. This is the most likely explanation for the 20% gap. The model learned patterns from biased training data and reproduced them. As the SageMaker documentation explains, models trained on data that reflects existing disparities can reproduce those disparities or even exacerbate them. What it is not A few tempting explanations don’t hold up: “ It’s just statistical noise from different sample sizes. ” Sample-size noise is random and usually small. A consistent gap of 20%+ across groups is a material disparity that demands investigation, not a rounding error. “
title: An 89% Accurate Hiring AI Can Still Be Unfair. Here’s Why.

summary: Four protocols walk into one project. An orchestrator that speaks AG-UI streams its answers as server-sent events, two specialists answer A2A tasks — one of them for 115 seconds past any synchronous read timeout — and a billing tool server answers MCP calls on EC2 instance types I chose myself. On top of the fleet sits a catalog: the Agent Registry, shared across accounts through RAM, whose semantic search finds the record named billing when asked for payment processing. Every number below was measured in one account, us-east-1 . The use case Northwind Gear's legal desk reviews supplier contracts. Two jobs keep the lawyers busy: a clause-by-clause read against the house wording, and a compliance screen that escalates anything policy-breaking. A contract-review orchestrator receives the brief and farms each job out to a specialist agent, because the two teams refuse to share a prompt, a model version, or a release schedule. Finance, meanwhile, wants one place where every agent and every MCP server the company runs is registered and findable — including from the shared services account — without asking engineering for a spreadsheet. What AgentCore does here Runtime hosts four agents, one per protocol: AG-UI for the orchestrator, A2A for the legal and compliance specialists, MCP for the billing tool server. A2A protocol carries the specialist traffic: blocking message/send for the quick review, non-blocking accept plus polling for the long scan, and message/stream with tasks/can
title: Two specialists, one orchestrator, one catalog

summary: The MySQL primary was still running. Applications could reach the database. Yet some write requests were taking too long and timing out. The problem wasn't a missing primary. Both replicas had stopped replicating, and semi-synchronous replication had become part of the availability problem. In Part 1 , I covered deploying MySQL with MOCO. Part 2 covered backups, MinIO, and a davfs2 failure. This time, let's look at the replication behavior that matters when things go wrong. The three-instance cluster MOCO uses GTID-based semi-synchronous replication for its normal three-instance MySQL clusters: one writable primary and two read-only replicas. Application | v eks-db-1 PRIMARY | binary log events / \ v v eks-db-0 eks-db-2 REPLICA REPLICA \ / replication ACK With asynchronous replication, the primary can acknowledge a committed transaction to the application without waiting for any replica to confirm receipt. With semi-synchronous replication, the primary waits for the configured number of replicas to acknowledge receiving the transaction's binary-log events . An ACK does not mean the replica has already applied the transaction. With MOCO's normal three-instance configuration, one replica acknowledgement is required. Losing one replica does not necessarily stop writes; the other can still acknowledge them. Losing both removes that acknowledgement path. The configuration that changes everything On the primary, these commands reveal the relevant settings: SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIK
title: Getting Started with MOCO Part 3: When MySQL Replicas Fail — Understanding Semi-Synchronous Replication

summary: A few months ago I was performing a cloud cost analysis for a project. One of the things that stood out during the analysis was the slowly increasing EC2-Other category in AWS Cost Explorer. After looking at the Usage Type, it appeared the size for EC2 snapshots storage was increasing day after day in the account. During the investigation it became apparent that this trend was visible across multiple accounts. Finding the root cause took a bit of investigation, so I decided to write it down in case others would run into the same problem. The workload The workload was an application running on Windows EC2 instances. In a central build account, a new version of the application would be installed on a predefined Windows version and baked into a new Amazon Machine Image (AMI). To do that, an EC2 Image Builder pipeline was created that ran on a daily schedule and resulted in a new AMI with a corresponding EBS volume. When the new AMI was created successfully by the pipeline, the AMI was distributed to other AWS accounts within the organization by means of the EC2 Image Builder pipeline feature called cross-account image distribution. Each day, a scheduled deployment would trigger and the deployment would replace the Windows EC2 with a new instance based on the latest published AMI, at which time the old AMI would become obsolete. Cross-account AMI distribution There are different ways to share AMIs with other accounts. In this project the setup was chosen to use cross-account AMI
title: How a missing IAM policy statement slowly increased the AWS bill

summary: A CloudWatch CPU alarm driving Systems Manager remediation through EventBridge, in two CloudFormation templates: a runbook and a direct Run Command target. An alarm on CPUUtilization above 90 percent, an EC2 instance registered as a managed node, and a shell script that has to run on the instance that breached. That is the whole scope, and the design everyone reaches for puts a CloudWatch alarm, an Amazon EventBridge rule, and an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook between the first two and the third. Run by hand, the same procedure is three steps and a judgement call: read the alarm, find the instance behind the data point, send the script to that instance and nothing else. The judgement call is the step that does not survive being automated carelessly, because it is the one that decides where the script lands. Send it to the wrong node and the remediation becomes the incident. The common design works. What it hides is a single assumption: that the identifier of the instance that breached travels from the metric to the action. Three of the six designs on the table cannot carry it at all, and the three that can carry it in three different ways, at three different prices. One of them pays with a host on the critical path, one pays with code to own, and the one I kept carries the value only because a specific JSON path happens to exist inside the alarm's own configuration snapshot. That path is the whole decision, and it is also the structural limit of the design. The condit

summary: Last month I lost half a day to a workflow that was working perfectly. It just was not running. An order-sync job on my self-hosted n8n had been switched off during an unrelated edit. No red execution. No error email. The dashboard was calm. The only reason I found it: someone asked why a downstream report looked stale. That is the gap. Nearly every monitoring guide for n8n starts with an error workflow. An error workflow is good at one job, and only that job: it fires when an execution fails. It does nothing when an execution never starts. This post is about that second case, the one most setups never alert on. I will show you why your error workflow is blind to it, then build a small liveness check that catches it, and I tested the whole thing on a production-shaped stack: n8n 2.43.6 on PostgreSQL 16 on an Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 box. Not the default SQLite demo. The same shape you actually run. This is a follow-up to my earlier post on securing self-hosted n8n on AWS . If you followed that one, this plugs the monitoring hole it leaves open. summary: Hola Amigos 👋 Welcome back to K8s-With-Pravesh! After covering the Datastore of Kubernetes: etcd , we're going deep into what is popularly known as the "Autopilot" of the Kubernetes Control Plane: the Controller Manager. We'll understand how it plays a crucial role in continuously reconciling the state of our cluster. For those of you who are new here, I'm Pravesh, an AWS Community Builder and IBM Champion. In this series, we're dissecting all the important components of a Kubernetes cluster. So, get your terminals ready, and let's dive right in! What is Kubernetes Controller Manager? The Kubernetes Controller Manager ( kube-controller-manager ) is a core component of the Control Plane that runs multiple built-in controllers within a single process. Each controller has a specific responsibility, but they all follow a similar mechanism: they continuously watch the state of the cluster, and whenever the actual state differs from the desired state, they take action to bring things back in sync. This process is popularly known as the Reconciliation Loop . The reconciliation loop operates through three major steps: Watch: Watches the API Server to get updates about the current state of the cluster. Compare: Compares the actual state against the desired state defined in the YAML configuration (which is stored in etcd). Act: If there is a mismatch (a "drift"), it takes action to correct it. summary: In 2021, Vodafone published a test every team arguing about performance should know. Two landing pages looked and worked the same, with paid traffic split 50/50, about 34,000 visits a day each. One version rendered its critical HTML on the server, moved a widget off the client and resized its hero image. Its Largest Contentful Paint was 31% better in field data (5.7 s against 8.3 s). That page sold 8% more, with 15% more leads and 11% more carts per visit ( web.dev ). Here's the part I like: 5.7 seconds is still "poor" by Google's thresholds (over 4). The winning page wasn't fast, just less slow, and people still bought more. So when someone says performance can wait until after launch, show them this. TL;DR Budget on percentiles (p95/p99), and say whether you mean latency or throughput. Averages hide the users you lose. Cache in layers (edge, application, database), picked by how fresh the data must be. Lambda cold starts hit under 1% of invocations (AWS), which is exactly your tail. Load-test with an open model and fail the build when p95 goes over budget. For LLM features, budget time-to-first-token , output tokens/sec and end-to-end p95 separately. Streaming and prompt caching are your biggest levers. What performance actually means Performance is how fast, and how much, work your system does for a user under a stated load. summary: Verified on 2026-11-04 against strands-agents 1.63.0, strands-agents-tools 0.8.11, mcp 2.3.0, Python 3.11 and Bedrock in us-east-1 . The model is deepseek.v3.2 on Amazon Bedrock. Article 01 showed how a tool's answer travels back to the model as a user-role message. This article is about the other direction: how the tool is described to the model in the first place. Read 01 first if you have not; everything here assumes the loop from it. The smallest tool that works A tool is a function with a decorator. This one counts lines of code under a directory. from strands import Agent , tool from strands.models import BedrockModel @tool def count_lines ( path : str , extension : str = " .py " ) -> int : """ Count total lines in all files with a given extension under a directory. summary: DISCLAIMER: This image is AI edited, because I don't want to expose my personal emails here! 🏃 TL;DR Sorry for the long post. I tried to cut it, but every paragraph I removed turned out to be a hole I would then have had to leave open. Yes, this is yet another Gmail assistant. I built it with Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and it lives on Telegram: it reads my mailbox, sends me a digest at 10:00, sets reminders tied to specific emails and remembers what I decide to ignore. Nothing new in November 2026. I built it to see what security work a simple agent needs once it reads private data, reads text written by strangers, and can act on both. I built it because it still amazes me how many agents are built, demoed and put in front of real users without anyone asking the right questions: what does this agent read, who wrote it, what can it do if it is fooled, and who would notice? Sadly, you would not be surprised by how easy it is to fool the model behind your favorite bot. I used my own mailbox because an email can say anything, including orders aimed at the model, and because the assistant does more than answer: it can move or trash mail, create reminders and send attachments to Telegram. This post is the list of those questions, the answers I built, and what I have not answered yet. At the end I check it against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and the one for Agentic Applications. The ratings are my own assessment, not a certification. davide-desio-eleva /

summary: I used EKS Pod Identity for cert-manager , the EBS CSI driver and Vault, then ended up with a plain IAM user for Elasticsearch snapshots. TL;DR: EKS Pod Identity is simpler than IRSA, and I use it wherever the software supports it. Elasticsearch’s bundled repository-s3 plugin was the exception. On Elasticsearch 8.15.0 , IRSA silently fell back to the node role and Pod Identity was rejected by the bundled AWS SDK, so snapshots run on a narrowly scoped IAM user stored in the Elasticsearch keystore. Newer Elasticsearch versions behave differently, so test yours before copying my choice. Figure 1. The three credential paths an Elasticsearch pod can use for S3 snapshots, and what happened on each. Why I Chose Pod Identity First I built a centralized logging platform on EKS (Elasticsearch through ECK, Filebeat, Vault, cert-manager , ingress-nginx ). Every component that talks to AWS needs credentials without static keys, which on EKS means IRSA or Pod Identity. Pod Identity removes most of the ceremony from IRSA: Capability IRSA EKS Pod Identity Cluster prerequisite IAM OIDC provider per cluster Pod Identity Agent add-on Role-to-ServiceAccount link ServiceAccount annotation EKS API association Role trust policy Cluster OIDC provider + ServiceAccount conditions pods.eks.amazonaws.com (reusable across clusters) Credential delivery Projected token exchanged with STS Link-local ag
title: EKS Pod Identity vs IRSA: Where It Works, and Where Elasticsearch’s S3 Snapshots Break It

summary: This article provides a step by step guide to running A2A agents on AWS and driving them with the A2A CLI. A Rust agent on the official A2A Rust SDK runs in an Amazon Lightsail container. A Strands agent on an Amazon Bedrock model runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and hands its work to the Rust agent. Both also run on a laptop, and one set of a2a commands checks all four. https://github.com/xbill9/rust-dev/tree/main/a2a-strands-aws The A2A CLI drove all four endpoints with the same commands, 16 of 16 checks passed, and the CLI also carried the call from the Strands agent to the Rust agent. The two agents speak different protocol versions: the Rust SDK serves A2A 1.0 and Strands serves A2A 0.3. The CLI reads both. Strands' own Python client reads only 0.3, so the Strands agent calls the Rust agent by running the same a2a binary the laptop uses. On AWS the CLI needs a login token, a session header and the full agent card URL, and nothing else changes. What Is Being Built? summary: 1. Tokenization Definition: Tokenization is the process of breaking down text into smaller units, called tokens, which can be words, subwords, or even individual characters. These tokens serve as the building blocks that AI models use to process and generate language. How It Works: A sentence like "Artificial Intelligence is powerful." The model tokenizes it into smaller units: Word-level tokenization: ["Artificial", "Intelligence", "is", "powerful", "."] Subword tokenization (e.g., Byte-Pair Encoding): ["Artifi", "cial", "Intelli", "gence", "is", "power", "ful", "."] Character-level tokenization: ["A", "r", "t", "i", "f", "i", "c", "i", "a", "l", ...] Why It Matters: Helps models understand and generate text efficiently. Handles out-of-vocabulary words by breaking them into subwords. Reduces complexity compared to processing raw text. 2. Context Window Definition: The context window refers to the maximum number of tokens an AI model can process at once when generating responses. It determines how much prior text the model "remembers" during inference. How It Works: If a model has a context window of 4,096 tokens, it can only consider the last 4,096 tokens when generating a response. Older parts of a conversation or document may be forgotten unless explicitly included in the prompt. Why It Matters: Short context windows (e.g., 512 tokens) limit long-form coherence. Larger context windows (e.g., 32,000+ tokens) improve memory and allow models to process entire documents in a s
title: Gen AI Concepts for Bedrock

summary: In Understanding Observability with OpenTelemetry and Coffee , I introduced the fundamentals of observability. In Native OpenTelemetry , I explored how OpenTelemetry generates and processes telemetry, how the OpenTelemetry Collector manages telemetry pipelines, and why understanding those pipelines matters when troubleshooting production issues. But what happens after telemetry leaves the Collector? Which tools store and analyze it? How do you connect these tools, and what should you consider before operating them in production? This article explores the open-source observability ecosystem, from the responsibilities of individual tools to the engineering decisions involved in running them together. OpenTelemetry isn't your observability backend OpenTelemetry is an open-source, vendor-neutral observability framework. It provides APIs, SDKs, instrumentation libraries, and tools for generating, collecting, and exporting telemetry such as metrics, logs, and traces. It also defines common data formats and semantic conventions that help applications describe telemetry consistently. However, OpenTelemetry isn't an observability backend. It doesn't replace the storage, query interfaces, and dashboards that teams use to investigate production issues. Those capabilities come from other tools. Think of OpenTelemetry as the system that standardizes how information leaves each part of the coffee shop. The observability tools help you examine that information and understand what happened.
title: Beyond the Collector: How the Open-Source Observability Stack Fits Together

summary: This article provides a step by step comparison of six inference serving engines on one Amazon EC2 G6 instance: llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, mistral.rs, a plain PyTorch engine and Google's LiteRT-LM, each serving Gemma 4 E2B on Google's QAT 4-bit weights from one NVIDIA L4. https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev The question is which engine to put on a G6 when one small model has the whole GPU. Each engine gets the same weights, the same prompts, the same 1-to-64-request load sweep and the same 1,319 GSM8K and 400 BFCL questions, and each is measured with and without Google's E2B drafter wherever the engine supports one. Every engine ran on one instance, one at a time, with the card to itself. The Results in Brief Answer quality barely moves between engines. GSM8K lands between 0.8954 and 0.9014 on the five CUDA engines with the drafter on or off, and every paired difference against llama.cpp is within the run-to-run range. LiteRT-LM scores level on GSM8K and lower on BFCL. For one request, five engines are within 8% of each other without a drafter (134.7 to 144.6 tokens per second end to end) and LiteRT-LM runs at 0.62 to 0.73x llama.cpp. The drafter decides the order: it gives vLLM 1.96x, llama.cpp 1.53x, SGLang 1.39x and LiteRT-LM 1.15x, and it slows mistral.rs to 0.95x. Under load the batching engines separate. At 64 requests of 128 tokens in and 512 out, vLLM reaches 3,716 tokens per second without a drafter and 4,516 with it, SGLang 2,967, mistral.rs 1,825 and llama.cpp 1,056
title: Six Serving Engines on One EC2 G6: Gemma 4 E2B on an NVIDIA L4

The backend uses the Strands Agents framework and Amazon Bedrock. For each chat request, it creates a fresh agent instance and gives it a set of service-specific tools implemented with Boto3. The application is designed to support operations teams with investigation and routine administration while keeping the scope of available actions explicit. Ask questions about infrastructure, health, security posture, and costs. Gather details from supported AWS services through dedicated tools. summary: A Pod can remain Pending even when an Amazon EKS cluster has healthy nodes. One common reason is that no eligible node has enough allocatable CPU to satisfy the Pod's request. In this hands-on experiment, we first deploy a Pod that requests 500m CPU. Kubernetes schedules it on an existing c6a.large node. We then recreate the Pod with a request of 4 CPUs. The existing node cannot accommodate that request, so the Pod becomes unschedulable and EKS Auto Mode provisions additional capacity. The experiment demonstrates how a Kubernetes resource request can influence node provisioning. It does not demonstrate scaling based on actual CPU utilization: the container runs sleep 3600 , which does not consume four CPUs. What we will observe The experiment follows these steps: Deploy a Pod requesting 500m CPU and 128Mi memory. Confirm that it runs on an existing c6a.large instance. Recreate the Pod with a 4 CPU request, leaving memory unchanged. Observe the FailedScheduling event with reason Insufficient cpu . Inspect the NodeClaim created by EKS Auto Mode. Verify that a new c6a.2xlarge instance joins the cluster and reaches Ready . Confirm that the Pod is scheduled on the new node. The c6a.2xlarge is the instance type observed in this run, not a guaranteed selection. EKS Auto Mode chooses capacity that satisfies the workload and the constraints of the applicable NodePool, subject to available offerings and capacity. title: Kubernetes CPU Requests in Amazon EKS Auto Mode

summary: I have spent most of my career on the boring, important part of data work: the pipelines that run at 2 a.m. and that nobody thinks about until they break. And I have always liked pipelines for one simple reason. They do not improvise. Give a workflow engine a schedule, a schema, and a known sequence of steps, and it will run the same plan every single day, without getting tired or distracted or "creative." That predictability is the whole point. It is also the reason I was skeptical when people started talking about putting AI agents in charge of data operations. This post is about where I landed. Short version: an agent is a great front door to a pipeline, but it should never be the thing that decides how the pipeline runs. The pipeline should keep that job. Here is how to set it up that way with AWS Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Why the boring part is still the hard part Pipelines are predictable on paper. In practice, the operational work around them is anything but. Late files arrive in Amazon S3 hours after the batch window closed. An API throttles during a busy week. Someone in finance messages the on-call channel: "Can you re-run yesterday's partition? We fixed a reference table." The pipeline itself is automated, but the control plane around it is still manual.
